## What is learning in ML?
- What really is machine learning - some data input that predicts some output you care about? How do I choose the prediction algorithm? I heard [`XGBoost is all you
need`](https://www.xgblog.ai/p/xgboost-is-all-you-need). Do we just throw XGBoost at all of our classification and regression problems? Maybe. We can also throw in k-means and maybe some reinforcement learning and then
we have all of what we need.
- But really we were partially right: machine learning takes some data input and returns a prediction. Does this dress make me look fat?  features [is_dress_black=1, can_see_toes=0] out[class1_youre_just_fat=1].
- More importantly, machine learning is about generalizing from examples well.
- How do we pick a good classifier or a good algorithm that can learn the examples and generalize well against unseen data?
- Let's first take a look at the components that we need to make the machine learn.

### Anatomy of a Learner
- Representation
	- The set of classifiers that can be learned, or the hypothesis space.
	- Examples: K-nearest neighbor, Naive Bayes, Decision Trees, Neural Networks.
- Evaluation
	- This is how you tell if the classifier is any good, or better than another classifier in your hypothesis space.
	- Examples: Accuracy, precision, recall, Squared Error.
- Optimization
	- Our hypothesis space may be very large, so we need a way to search among that space to find the best classifier.
	- Examples: Greedy Search, Gradient Descent, Linear Programming.

```
   learner  =  Representation  +  Evaluation  +  Optimization
   -----------------------------------------------------------
                what shapes       how to score    how to search
                it can take       a candidate     the space
                KNN, trees        accuracy, MSE   gradient descent
```

- The model, like XGBoost, is only part of the learning. We are slightly joking about XGBoost but it is non-jokingly
good at a wide variety of tasks because it casts a large hypothesis space (set of possible solutions) by using many
weak learners (more on this later) and has built-in regularization **cough** generalization **cough**.

## Generalization is what matters
- Ok, we are ready to throw XGBoost and let it handle our optimization for us.

- Why does generalization even matter? Train/Val/Test and cross validation is engrained in our heads, but what if we just skip that? But then we will overfit. Why
is overfitting bad? Well, because the real goal of machine learning is to generalize beyond the data we have to train against.

- Generalization matters because we will very likely never see the same data during test time that you saw in training. The paper gives an example for a spam filter that
has 100,000 words, so there are 2^100,000 different possible inputs. You will never have the ability to train against all possible inputs, so your model needs to generalize
so it performs well against unseen input.

- The limits to the training examples mean that data alone is not enough, and that every learner must embody some knowledge or assumptions beyond the data it's given
in order to generalize beyond it. This also means choosing a representation means picking one that can fit to the domain knowledge.
	- Take for example a house price prediction: the data alone isn't enough; the representation bakes in an assumption.
	- Something like K-Nearest-Neighbor assumes locality - similar houses have similar prices.
	- Whereas a global linear function assumes price is one global formula over features.
	- Domain experts already know this to some level; appraisers look at nearby comps to determine the price of your home.
- In order to generalize there is a balance between a simple and complex representation. Our error can exist as incorrect assumptions about the data where we oversimplify the
relationship between features and class. At the opposite end of the complexity spectrum we can overfit, fit to the signal AND the noise, resulting in high variance.

``` {.python .cell-code}

results = run()       # prints the bias^2 / variance / total-error table
plot_fits(results);   # embeds the figure inline
```

-------------------------------------------------------
  1 |  0.1847 |  0.0011 |  0.0100 |  0.1957 |   0.1963
  3 |  0.0058 |  0.0026 |  0.0100 |  0.0184 |   0.0183
 12 |  0.0049 |  3.5744 |  0.0100 |  3.5893 |   3.5886

The `sum` column dips then explodes - that U-shape *is* the bias-variance tradeoff.
Degree 1 is all bias (underfit), degree 12's variance blows up (overfit), degree 3
is the sweet spot. Both the table and the figure above come straight from
[`bias_variance_decomp.py`](https://github.com/treeahsee/treeahsee.github.io/blob/main/bias_variance_decomp.py).

- Generalization becomes harder in higher dimensions as well. As the dimensions grow, the training set covers a dwindling fraction of your input space. In high
dimensions all examples start to look alike.

## What do we do about it?

- So how do we get a learner to actually generalize? There are a few ways:
	- inject more knowledge through features and domain intuition
	- inject more evidence through more data, let the data constrain the hypothesis
	- inject more models, combine many instead of betting on one

### Features
- The most important factor in a machine learning project is the features used.
- Features that look irrelevant in isolation may be relevant in combination.
- This is where machine learning in practice mixes both art and science; there is a lot of trial and error in feature design.
- We talked about how our representation can limit or give us the ability to model the domain, but feature engineering is
also where we can add our domain intuition to modeling the data.
- Features in isolation may look irrelevant but be relevant in combination.
	- XOR is a canonical case for this.
	- Look at A or B by itself and it tells you nothing more than random chance.
	- Modeling A & B together determines the class perfectly.

```
   A  B | A XOR B      A alone  -> 50/50, tells you nothing
   -----+--------      B alone  -> 50/50, tells you nothing
   0  0 |    0
   0  1 |    1         irrelevant apart,
   1  0 |    1         decisive together
   1  1 |    0
```

- Running a learner with many features and figuring out which one is important can also be done, but is time consuming.

### Moar Data
- Usually more data beats a more clever algorithm.
- Different learners can carve very different decision boundaries but still classify most new points the same way.
- So to a first approximation, once you have enough data, which algorithm you picked matters less than getting more of it.
- Fixed size learners vs learners that grow with the data
	- parametric: fixed capacity - add more samples and the number of parameters doesn't grow. A linear classifier with 11 features, if you give it an extra 100,000 training samples, still has 11 features.
	- non parametric: move a decision tree from 100 samples and 5 splits to 100,000 samples and the tree can grow 100's of levels deep.

### Ensembles
- Combining many learners, as opposed to the best single learner, often can result in much better results.
- Bagging
	- train many models in parallel on bootstrap resamples, then average/vote. Reduces variance. Random forests are this (plus random feature subsets).
- Boosting
	- train models sequentially; each new learner focuses on the examples previous ones got wrong, then weight them. Reduces bias (push it too far and it can overfit).

```
   Bagging (parallel)                 Boosting (sequential)
   cuts variance                      cuts bias

     [M1]  \                            [M1] -> [M2] -> [M3]
     [M2]  --> vote / average                each learner fixes
     [M3]  /                                 the last one's errors

   models trained independently       models build on each other
```

### Simpler isn't always better
- If two models have the same accuracy but one is simpler than the other, do you take the simple one? Maybe, but for other reasons than accuracy - for example maybe for interpretability, but
just because it's simpler doesn't mean it will generalize better. We see this in the ensembles where adding many learners may add complexity but lead to better predictability.

## Wrap up
- So, XGBoost isn't all you need. Darn - we actually need to think about the domain we are modeling and getting enough examples.
- We learned generalization is the name of the game; we need the model to learn signals that apply beyond the training set. There are many techniques that help us do this. A few this
paper shows were picking the right representation by thinking through your hypothesis space and the limits of the number of potential solutions, how your model grows with the data (nonparametric
vs parametric), getting high quality features and engineering to your domain knowledge, and striking a balance on model complexity.
